title: Freelance Rate Increase Kit
description: Raise your rates with existing clients without awkward negotiations: a rate review worksheet with worked maths, a client-by-client review tracker, a 90-day timeline, ten notice and follow-up emails from standard to stepped to a professional exit, scripts for eight common replies, and wording that makes future increases routine.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Rate Increase Kit

Raise your rates with the clients you already have, without awkward
negotiations or surprise exits. This kit takes you from "I should really
charge more" to a sent notice in about two hours: the numbers, the
decision for each client, the emails, and what to say when they reply.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| rate-review-worksheet.md | Work out your target rate and each client's new rate, with a worked example | 45 min, once a year |
| client-rate-review.csv | One row per client: current rate, gap, new rate, notice date, decision | 20 min |
| rate-increase-timeline.md | A 90-day plan from review to first invoice at the new rate | Read once, then tick off |
| rate-increase-emails.md | Ten emails: standard notice, retainer, stepped increase, budget heads-up, reminder, confirmation and a professional exit | Copy and adapt |
| reply-scripts.md | Calm answers to the eight replies clients most often send | Copy as needed |
| rate-review-wording.md | Plain lines for proposals, contracts and invoices so future increases are expected | 10 min |

## How to use it

1. **Know your number.** Fill in Part 1 of rate-review-worksheet.md to
   find the hourly rate your business actually needs. If you already know
   it, skip to Part 2.
2. **Review each client.** Add every active client to
   client-rate-review.csv. The worksheet shows how to choose between a
   standard increase, a stepped increase, holding the rate, or letting
   the client go.
3. **Plan the dates.** Use rate-increase-timeline.md to set an effective
   date with enough notice. 30 days is the minimum; 60 is better for
   retainers.
4. **Send the notice.** Pick the matching email from
   rate-increase-emails.md, fill in the brackets, and send it in writing.
5. **Answer replies calmly.** Use reply-scripts.md. Decide your fallback
   for each client before you send anything, not after.
6. **Make it routine.** Add the lines from rate-review-wording.md to your
   proposals and contracts, and put next year's review date in your
   calendar.

## Opening the CSV file

client-rate-review.csv opens in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or
LibreOffice. The example rows show how to fill it in; delete them when
you're ready. The gap_percent column is (target_rate - current_rate) /
current_rate x 100. To have the spreadsheet calculate it, replace the
example values with a formula such as =ROUND((D2-C2)/C2*100,0).

## Before you start

- Read your existing contracts. If a contract fixes your rate for a
  period or sets a notice requirement, follow it.
- Figures in the examples are illustrations. Your rates depend on your
  field, location, experience and demand.
- This kit is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice. If
  you're unsure about contract terms, ask a qualified adviser where you
  work.
files.rate-review-worksheet.md:
# Rate Review Worksheet

Do this once a year, on the same date. It has three parts: your target
rate, each client's new rate, and what to do with clients far below it.

---

## Part 1: Your target hourly rate

Fill in the blanks. Use yearly figures.

| Line | What to enter | Your figure |
|---|---|---|
| A | Income you want to pay yourself before tax | ______ |
| B | Business costs (software, equipment, insurance, accountant, training, coworking) | ______ |
| C | Money to set aside for tax on A (ask an adviser or use last year's actual rate) | ______ |
| D | Profit buffer for slow months and savings (10-15% of A is common) | ______ |
| E | **Total you need to bring in** (A + B + C + D) | ______ |
| F | Working weeks per year (52 minus holidays, public holidays, sick days, training) | ______ |
| G | Billable hours per working week (not total hours: leave out admin, sales, email) | ______ |
| H | **Billable hours per year** (F x G) | ______ |
| I | **Target hourly rate** (E / H) | ______ |

### Worked example

| Line | Figure |
|---|---|
| A | $54,000 |
| B | $6,000 |
| C | $13,500 |
| D | $6,500 |
| E | $80,000 |
| F | 44 weeks |
| G | 24 hours |
| H | 1,056 hours |
| I | $75.76, rounded to **$75** (the buffer in line D covers the difference) |

Most people overestimate line G. If you don't know your real billable
hours, log your time for two weeks before you finish this part. 20-28
billable hours in a 40-hour week is common for solo freelancers.

---

## Part 2: Each client's new rate

For each client, write their current rate and how long since it last
changed. Then work out the gap:

    gap % = (target rate - current rate) / current rate x 100

Use the gap to choose an approach:

| Gap | Last change | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| 0% or less | any | **Hold.** No change this round. |
| 1-10% | any | **Standard.** Move to your target rate in one step. |
| 11-25% | any | **Standard, stepped or restructure.** One step if the relationship is strong; two steps six months apart if not; or a new retainer or project price at the target rate (Part 3). |
| Over 25% | any | **Stepped or review.** Two steps, a change of structure, or a decision about whether to keep the client (Part 3). |

Round every new rate to a clean number ($65, $70, $72.50 for half-hour
billing). Odd figures like $66.42 look like they came from a formula,
which invites a conversation about the formula.

### Worked example: four clients, target rate $75

| Client | Current | Last change | Gap | Approach | New rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harbour Studio | $70 | 14 months ago | 7% | Standard | $75 from 1 Feb |
| Linden Books | $60 | 24 months ago | 25% | Stepped | $67 from 1 Feb, $75 from 1 Aug |
| Northgate Clinic (retainer) | $1,200/month for 20 hrs ($60/hr) | 12 months ago | 25% | Restructure | $1,350/month for 18 hrs ($75/hr) from 1 Mar |
| Quayside Events | $50 | 30 months ago | 50% | Review | See Part 3 |

What it adds up to, assuming hours stay the same:

| Client | Hours/month | Extra per month | Extra per year |
|---|---|---|---|
| Harbour Studio | 10 | $50 | $600 |
| Linden Books | 20 | $140, then $300 | $2,640 in year one |
| Northgate Clinic | 18 (was 20) | $150 | $1,800, and 2 hours a month back |
| **Total** | | | **$5,040** |

The names are invented for the example.

---

## Part 3: Clients far below your rate

When a client is more than 25% below your target rate, answer these
questions honestly:

1. If this client left, could I fill their hours at my target rate within
   three months?  Yes / No / Not sure
2. Does this client bring something other than money (referrals, a
   portfolio piece, reliable payment, easy work)?  Yes / No
3. How many hours a month do they take?  ______
4. What would those hours earn at my target rate?  ______

Then choose:

- **Step up.** Two increases announced in one message (email 3). Best
  when the client values you and the answer to question 2 is yes.
- **Restructure.** Move to a monthly retainer or a fixed project price at
  the new level (email 4). Best when the work is predictable.
- **Hold, with a date.** Keep the current rate for six more months, then
  review again. Best when you can't fill the time yet. Write the review
  date in client-rate-review.csv so it doesn't drift again.
- **Part ways.** Give the increase, accept that they may leave, and offer
  a clean handover (email 9). Best when the answer to question 1 is yes.

### Worked example: Quayside Events

- 12 hours a month at $50 = $600 a month.
- At $75, those hours would earn $900 a month.
- The freelancer has a waiting list of two enquiries, so question 1 is yes.
- Quayside pays late and the work isn't portfolio quality, so question 2
  is no.

Decision: send a stepped notice ($62 from 1 Feb, $75 from 1 Aug) and be
ready to part ways if they decline. If they leave, the 12 hours go to a
client on the waiting list at $75.

---

## Your fallback, decided in advance

For each client, write one line before you send the notice:

    If [client] says no, I will ______________________.

Choices: accept a short delay (up to __ weeks), reduce scope to fit their
budget, hold for six months, or end the work with a handover. Deciding
now stops you from agreeing to something under pressure later.

files.rate-increase-timeline.md:
# Rate Increase Timeline

A 90-day plan from "I need to raise my rates" to the first invoice at the
new rate. Count backwards from your effective date. If you're short on
time, the minimum is 30 days' notice for hourly clients and 60 for
retainers.

Example dates assume an effective date of 1 February.

---

## Day -90 to -75 (early November): Review

- [ ] Read every active contract. Note any fixed-rate period, notice
      requirement or renewal date in client-rate-review.csv.
- [ ] Complete Part 1 of rate-review-worksheet.md to set your target rate.
- [ ] Add every active client to client-rate-review.csv with their
      current rate and the date it last changed.
- [ ] Note which clients plan budgets for next year now. If any do, send
      email 5 (budget heads-up) this week.

## Day -75 to -60 (mid November): Decide

- [ ] Choose an approach for each client: hold, standard, stepped,
      restructure or part ways (Parts 2 and 3 of the worksheet).
- [ ] Write the new rate for each client, rounded to a clean number.
- [ ] Write your fallback for each client in the fallback_if_no column.
- [ ] For retainer clients, send the notice now (email 2 or 4): they get
      60 days or more.

## Day -60 to -45 (early to mid December): Notify

- [ ] Send notices to hourly and project clients (email 1 or 3).
- [ ] Send in writing, even if you also mention it on a call.
- [ ] Record the date sent in the notice_sent column.
- [ ] Avoid sending in the last week before a major holiday, when
      messages get buried. If that's when your dates land, send earlier.

## Day -45 to -14 (mid December to mid January): Reply

- [ ] Reply to every response within two working days, using
      reply-scripts.md.
- [ ] Record each reply and outcome in the CSV.
- [ ] If a client hasn't acknowledged the notice after 14 days, send
      email 6 (gentle check).

## Day -14 to -7 (mid to late January): Confirm

- [ ] Send email 7 (reminder) to every client whose rate is changing.
- [ ] Update your invoice template, quote template and any rate card.
- [ ] If you use time-tracking or invoicing software, set the new rate to
      start on the effective date.
- [ ] Check that any work already quoted at the old rate is clearly
      marked so it's invoiced at the agreed price.

## Day 0 (1 February): Effective

- [ ] New rate applies to new work and new hours from today.
- [ ] Send email 8 (thank-you confirmation) to clients who accepted, if
      you didn't already.

## Day +1 to +30 (February): First invoice

- [ ] Send the first invoice at the new rate. Show the rate clearly on
      the invoice so there's no surprise.
- [ ] If a client pays the old amount, reply promptly and politely with
      the difference and a reference to your notice. Most of the time
      it's an accounts team using an old figure.

## Day +180 (August): Second step, if stepped

- [ ] Send email 7 (reminder) 30 days before any second step.
- [ ] Update templates and software for the second rate.

## Every year

- [ ] Put next year's review date in your calendar now, on the same date
      as this year's.
- [ ] Record it in the next_review column of the CSV.

---

## If you only have 30 days

1. Day -30: Set your target rate and new rates (one hour).
2. Day -30: Send email 1 to every client whose rate is changing.
3. Day -14: Send email 6 to anyone who hasn't replied.
4. Day -7: Send email 7 and update your templates.
5. Day 0: Invoice at the new rate.

Retainer clients should get more than 30 days. If you can't give 60,
consider starting their increase one billing cycle later than everyone
else's.
files.rate-increase-emails.md:
# Rate Increase Emails

Ten emails covering the whole process. Replace everything in
[brackets]. Keep them short: the shorter the notice, the more settled it
sounds.

Three rules for every email:

1. **State the rate and the date plainly.** No "around" or "early next
   year".
2. **One sentence of reason, at most.** You don't need to justify running
   your business.
3. **Offer to talk, don't ask permission.** "Happy to set up a call" not
   "Would that be okay?"

---

## 1. Standard notice (hourly or ad hoc client)

**Subject:** My rates from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for another good year working on [project or area]. [One specific
thing that went well, e.g. "The spring campaign was a highlight for
me."]

I'm writing to let you know that from [1 February], my rate for ongoing
work will be [$75] an hour, up from [$70]. I review my rates once a year,
and this reflects my current costs and the time I put into each piece of
work.

Anything we've agreed before then will stay at the current rate. If
you'd like to talk about scope or budget for the year ahead, I'm happy
to set up a quick call.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 2. Retainer notice

**Subject:** Your retainer from [1 March]

Hi [Name],

I've really valued working with you on [area] this year, especially
[specific result].

I'm writing with plenty of notice to let you know that from [1 March],
the monthly retainer will be [$1,350], up from [$1,200]. Everything else
stays the same: [the same scope / the same response times / the same
monthly report].

Your [January and February] invoices will be at the current rate. If
you'd like to adjust the scope to fit next year's budget, let me know and
I'll suggest a couple of options.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 3. Stepped increase (client well below your rate)

**Subject:** Rates for [2027]

Hi [Name],

Thank you for [length of time] of work together on [area]. [Specific
thing you're proud of.]

My rate for you hasn't changed since we started, and it's now some way
below what I charge for similar work. Rather than make one large change,
I'd like to move in two steps:

- From [1 February]: [$67] an hour (currently [$60])
- From [1 August]: [$75] an hour

That gives you time to plan for both. Work already agreed will stay at
the current rate.

If it would help to talk through priorities for the year, I'm happy to
set up a call.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 4. Restructure (move to a new retainer or package at the new rate)

**Subject:** A simpler way to work together next year

Hi [Name],

Looking back at the last [12 months], most months we've worked about
[20] hours on [type of work]. I'd like to move us to a monthly package
from [1 March], which makes budgeting simpler on your side and lets me
plan time for you properly.

What I'm proposing:

- [18] hours a month of [type of work]
- [What's included, e.g. "one strategy call and a short monthly report"]
- [$1,350] a month, invoiced at the start of each month
- Extra hours at [$75] an hour, agreed in advance

This replaces our current hourly arrangement at [$60] an hour. I'm happy
to talk through the details or adjust what's included.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 5. Budget heads-up (send before the client plans next year)

**Subject:** Quick note for your [2027] planning

Hi [Name],

I know [this is around the time / you mentioned] you plan budgets for
next year, so I wanted to give you an early heads-up: from [1 February]
my rate will be [$75] an hour, up from [$70].

If it would help, I can send a rough estimate of next year's work based
on this year's hours, so you have a number to plan with.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 6. Gentle check (no reply after 14 days)

**Subject:** Re: My rates from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

Just checking this reached you, since it affects your invoices from
[1 February]. No action needed unless you'd like to talk anything
through.

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 7. Reminder (7-14 days before the change)

**Subject:** Reminder: new rate from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

A quick reminder that my new rate of [$75] an hour starts on
[1 February], as mentioned in my note on [date]. Invoices for work from
that date will show the new rate.

[If relevant: "The [project] we agreed in December will be invoiced at
the original quote."]

Thanks,
[Your name]

---

## 8. Thank-you confirmation (client accepted)

**Subject:** Re: My rates from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for coming back to me so quickly, and for the continued work. I'm
looking forward to [next project or area] in the new year.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 9. Professional exit (client can't accept, you're parting ways)

**Subject:** Re: My rates from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for letting me know, and I completely understand.

I'm not able to continue at the current rate, so I'd suggest we wrap up
our work together by [date]. Before then I'll:

- finish [current tasks]
- send you [files, logins, documentation] in one place
- [introduce you to someone else / share a short handover note] if that
  would help

It's been a pleasure working with you, and if things change in future
I'd be glad to hear from you.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 10. Agreed delay (you've accepted a short postponement)

**Subject:** Re: My rates from [1 February]

Hi [Name],

Happy to help with that. I'll keep the current rate until [1 March], and
the new rate of [$75] an hour will apply from then. I'll note it on your
invoices so it's clear.

Thanks,
[Your name]
files.reply-scripts.md:
# Reply Scripts

How to answer the eight replies clients most often send after a rate
increase notice. The aim is always the same: keep the new rate, keep the
relationship, and stay calm.

Before you reply to anything, check the fallback you wrote in
client-rate-review.csv. Don't decide under pressure.

---

## 1. "Can we keep the old rate a bit longer?"

**What it usually means:** They've already budgeted this quarter, or the
person who approves spending needs time.

**Reply:**

> That's no problem. I can hold the current rate until [1 March], and the
> new rate will apply from then.

**Why it works:** You agree to a date, not to dropping the increase.
Offer a delay of weeks, not months. Then send email 10.

---

## 2. "Our budget is fixed."

**What it usually means:** They want to keep working with you but can't
spend more.

**Reply:**

> I understand. At the new rate, your current budget of [$1,200] a month
> covers about [16] hours instead of [20]. Shall we look at which tasks
> matter most so the budget goes to those first?

**Why it works:** You change the scope, not the price. Many clients
discover some of the work wasn't essential.

---

## 3. "Other freelancers charge less."

**What it usually means:** They're testing whether the increase is firm.

**Reply:**

> That may well be true, and I understand you need to get good value.
> After [two years] I know your [audience, systems, style] well, which
> saves us both time on every piece of work. My rate from [1 February]
> will be [$75], and I'd be glad to keep working together at that rate.

**Why it works:** You don't argue about other people's prices. You name
the specific value of continuity and leave the decision with them.

---

## 4. "Can you meet us in the middle?"

**What it usually means:** A genuine attempt to negotiate.

**Options, depending on your fallback:**

- **Hold firm:** "I've set this rate across all my clients, so I'd rather
  keep it consistent. I can hold the current rate until [date] if timing
  helps."
- **Step it:** "I could do [$70] from [1 February] and [$75] from
  [1 August]. Would that work for planning?"
- **Trade something:** "I can keep [$70] if we move to a monthly package
  of [15] hours paid at the start of each month."

**Why it works:** If you give something, get something: time, commitment,
or upfront payment.

---

## 5. "Why now?" or "What's changed?"

**What it usually means:** They want a reason they can pass on to
whoever approves the budget.

**Reply:**

> I review my rates once a year to keep them in line with my costs and
> the market for this kind of work. It's been [18 months] since your rate
> last changed. Happy to put that in a short note for your finance team if
> it helps.

**Why it works:** A routine reason is easy for them to repeat
internally. Avoid personal reasons.

---

## 6. "We'll need to think about it."

**What it usually means:** They need approval, or they're considering
alternatives.

**Reply:**

> Of course. The new rate applies from [1 February], so let me know by
> [two weeks before] if you'd like to talk about scope or timing before
> then.

**Why it works:** You give a clear date to reply by, without pushing.

---

## 7. "We can't do it. We'll have to stop."

**What it usually means:** It's a genuine no, or a final test.

**Reply (if your fallback is to part ways):** Use email 9 (professional
exit).

**Reply (if your fallback is to hold):**

> I appreciate you being straightforward with me. I'd like to keep
> working together, so I'll hold your current rate until [date], and we
> can review it again then.

Write the new review date in the CSV straight away.

**Why it works:** Either way, you're acting on a decision you made in
advance, not reacting.

---

## 8. No reply at all

**What it usually means:** The email was missed, or they've accepted it
without comment.

**What to do:** After 14 days, send email 6 (gentle check). Seven to
fourteen days before the effective date, send email 7 (reminder). Then
invoice at the new rate. Silence after two written notices is generally
treated as acceptance in day-to-day business, but if your contract says
otherwise, follow your contract.

---

## If a client pays the old amount

> Hi [Name], thanks for the payment. It looks like invoice [number] was
> paid at the previous rate of [$70] an hour rather than [$75], which
> started on [1 February] (my note of [date] is below). Could you send
> the difference of [$50] when you next run payments? Thanks!

Attach or paste your original notice. It's usually an accounts team
using an old figure.
files.rate-review-wording.md:
# Rate Review Wording

The easiest rate increase is one the client already expects. Add these
plain-language lines to your proposals, contracts and invoices so every
future increase is routine.

These are general examples, not legal advice. Contract law varies by
country and situation. If you're relying on a clause, have a qualified
adviser where you work check your contract.

---

## In proposals

Pick one and add it near your pricing.

- "Rates are reviewed once a year in [January]. I'll always give at least
  30 days' written notice of any change."
- "This quote is valid for 30 days. Work agreed after that date will be
  priced at my rates at the time."
- "Fixed-price projects are always invoiced at the quoted price, even if
  my rates change while the project is running."

## In contracts or terms of business

Example wording to discuss with your adviser:

> **Rate reviews.** The Freelancer may review the hourly rate (or monthly
> fee) once in each 12-month period. The Freelancer will give the Client
> at least [30] days' written notice of any change. Work agreed in writing
> before the change takes effect will be charged at the rate in force when
> it was agreed.

For retainers:

> **Retainer fee.** The monthly fee may be reviewed on each anniversary of
> the start date. The Freelancer will give at least [60] days' written
> notice of any change. Either party may end the retainer by giving
> [30] days' written notice.

## On invoices

A single line in the footer, from about three months before your review
date:

- "Please note: rates are reviewed annually in [January]."

And from the effective date:

- "Rate from [1 February 2027]: [$75] per hour."

## In your onboarding email for new clients

> One practical note: I review my rates once a year in [January] and
> always give at least 30 days' notice. Anything we've already agreed
> stays at the agreed price.

## On your rate card or website

- "Rates from [1 February 2027]. Reviewed annually."

---

## Why this works

- The client hears about rate reviews when they hire you, not when the
  review arrives.
- A fixed annual date makes the increase feel routine rather than
  personal.
- Promising to honour agreed work protects trust: clients know a quote
  is a quote.
